docs.title: Legal Ontologies Foundry
docs.text:
The Legal Ontologies Foundry (LOF) is a collaborative initiative to develop interoperable, logically well-formed ontologies for the legal domain. Following the model of the OBO Foundry, member ontologies share a common upper ontology (Basic Formal Ontology, ISO/IEC 21838-2), a common format (OWL 2), persistent identifiers, and a common set of principles. As a result, models of obligations, rights, roles, institutions, legal acts, and evidence built by different groups can be combined without translation loss.

Founding draft

This site is in its founding phase. The principles, policies, and governance pages are drafts for ratification by the founding coordinators. Proposed changes are welcome as pull requests or in Discussions.

Get involved

The Foundry is open to anyone working on law, ontology, or legal information systems, and we especially welcome input before the founding coordinators' next meeting. Four ways to start, none needing any commitment:

  1. Review a design pattern. Read one of the four draft patterns and comment at the foot of its page or in Discussions.
  2. Tell us about an existing legal ontology that should be in the registry, or a vocabulary we should align with.
  3. Bring a use case. A worked example from your jurisdiction or practice is one of the most useful things anyone can contribute.
  4. Pick up a starter task. Issues labeled good first issue are small and self-contained.

To see what is under discussion right now, without GitHub, read the Activity pages: open proposals, discussions, the decision log, and members, refreshed every hour.

No GitHub account? You can do all of this through a simple form: see Take part without GitHub.

Comments at the foot of each page need only a free GitHub account. See Contributing for more.

docs.title: Why a foundry
docs.text: Legal information systems, from court records and statutory databases to compliance tools and AI systems that reason about law, increasingly depend on machine-readable representations of legal entities. Existing legal vocabularies were developed largely in isolation, with incompatible upper-level commitments, which makes them difficult to integrate or audit. The Foundry applies the methods that have succeeded in the biomedical sciences: shared principles, coordinated development, public review, and orthogonal ontologies that each cover a well-delimited domain.

docs.title: First contributions
docs.text:
You do not need to be an ontologist or a programmer to help. Useful first contributions include:

  • Commenting on a design pattern. Is a definition clear? Does the pattern fit a case from your legal system? Comment at the foot of the page, or in Discussions.
  • Suggesting a legal ontology or vocabulary for the registry or for alignment, with a link and its license.
  • Contributing a worked example: a lease, an appointment, a statute and its implementing regulation, from your jurisdiction.
  • Adding a reading to the Literature pages.

Issues labeled good first issue are small, self-contained starting points. If you are unsure where something goes, open a thread in Discussions and a coordinator will help.

docs.title: Editing a page
docs.text:
1. Click the pencil icon at the top of any page.
  2. GitHub opens the Markdown source. Make your edit.
  3. Describe the change and choose Propose changes. This creates a pull request.
  4. A coordinator reviews and merges it, and the site rebuilds automatically.

The registry and ontology detail pages are generated: to change them, edit the ontology's metadata file in ontology/ instead.

docs.title: Code of Conduct
docs.text: The Legal Ontologies Foundry brings together philosophers, lawyers, computer scientists, and practitioners who disagree, often productively, about foundational questions. This code exists to keep that disagreement useful.

docs.title: Expected conduct
docs.text:
• Argue about ideas, not people. Criticism of a model, definition, or principle is welcome; personal attacks are not.
  • Assume good faith, and ask for clarification before concluding that someone is wrong.
  • Credit the work of others (see LOF-P-018).
  • Keep discussion relevant to the forum it is in.

docs.title: Unacceptable conduct
docs.text: Harassment, discriminatory language, threats, sustained disruption of discussion, and publishing others' private information are not acceptable in any Foundry space: repositories, issue trackers, Discussions, meetings, or mailing lists.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text: Report concerns privately to any Operations Committee member. Reports are handled confidentially. The committee may warn, temporarily restrict, or remove participants who violate this code.

docs.title: How does the Foundry relate to the OBO Foundry?
docs.text: The Legal Ontologies Foundry adopts the OBO Foundry's methods: shared principles, a common upper ontology (BFO), persistent identifiers, a public registry, and coordinated review. It applies them to the legal domain, which OBO does not cover. See related initiatives.

docs.title: Do I have to accept a particular theory of law to contribute?
docs.text: No. The Foundry requires that legal entities be grounded in BFO and that the grounding be explicit and argued (LOF-P-004). It does not require any particular jurisprudential theory. Competing groundings can be documented and compared through the design pattern series.

docs.title: Can an ontology cover only one jurisdiction?
docs.text: Yes. Many will. LOF-P-010 requires only that jurisdiction-specific content be labeled as such.

docs.title: Why w3id.org rather than our own domain?
docs.text: w3id.org is a community-maintained, permanent redirect service. It lets the Foundry move its hosting without breaking any identifier. See identifiers.

docs.title: Can I use Foundry ontologies commercially?
docs.text: Yes. All Foundry ontologies are released under CC BY 4.0 or CC0 (LOF-P-001).

docs.title: How do I propose a new ontology?
docs.text: Follow the new ontology request SOP.

docs.title: Governance
docs.text:
Draft for ratification

This page takes effect when each founding coordinator has approved the pull request that adopts it.

The Foundry's structure follows the OBO Foundry model: an Operations Committee with overall responsibility, and working groups that carry out the work.

docs.title: Operations Committee
docs.text:
During the founding phase the Operations Committee consists of the founding coordinators:

  • David R. Koepsell
  • William Mandrick
  • Barry Smith

The Operations Committee is responsible for the principles, the registry, the w3id.org/lof namespace, admission decisions, and appointments to working groups. It meets as needed and records decisions in this repository.

docs.title: Working groups
docs.text: See Working groups.

docs.title: Decision-making
docs.text:
1. Routine changes (typo fixes, clarifications, new registry entries at draft status, updates to an ontology's own metadata) need approval from one Operations Committee member on the pull request.
  2. Substantive changes (new or amended principles or policies, admission to accepted status, changes to the identifier scheme, changes to this page) need approval from all Operations Committee members, after a comment period of at least 14 days announced in Discussions.
  3. The committee aims for consensus. A substantive change on which consensus cannot be reached is not adopted.

The pull-request history of this repository is the Foundry's official record of decisions.

docs.title: Ontology status
docs.text: The metadata policy defines the two status fields, status (draft, candidate, accepted, deprecated) and activity_status (active, inactive, orphaned). Status changes follow the review SOP.

docs.title: Transition beyond the founding phase
docs.text: Once the Foundry has at least five accepted ontologies maintained by at least three independent groups, the Operations Committee will propose a standing structure with elected, rotating membership, for adoption under the rules above.

docs.title: Conduct
docs.text: All participation is governed by the Code of Conduct.

docs.title: Working groups
docs.text: Working groups are appointed by the Operations Committee. During the founding phase, the committee members may lead working groups themselves. Each group has a lead, who reports to the committee.

docs.title: Technical Working Group
docs.text:

Welcome to the Legal Ontologies Foundry

The Foundry is building open, interoperable legal ontologies on Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), modeled on the OBO Foundry. Everything here is a draft for discussion, and input from anyone working on law, ontology, or legal information systems is welcome, especially before the founding coordinators' next meeting.

Good places to start: - Read the four draft design patterns: https://legal-ontologies-foundry.github.io/odp/ - Introduce yourself in this thread: who you are, and what brings you here - Pick up a starter task: issues labeled "good first issue" - Ask anything in Q&A; no question is too basic

David Koepsell, William Mandrick, and Barry Smith

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Fill in the form. It asks for your name, your email address, and what you want to say.
  2. We email you a confirmation link. Nothing is posted until you click it. This keeps out spam and makes sure no one posts in your name.

  • Claimant Role: A Deontic Role that inheres in an Agent A, that mutually depends on the existence of a Duty Holder Role borne by Agent B, and that specifies B performing or abstaining from some Act C, or providing or surrendering some Continuant D to A.

  • Deontic Declaration Performer Role: A Role inhering in an Agent or Aggregate of Agents that is realized by the bearer being the active participant (agent in) a Deontic Declaration.

  • Deontic Power Role: A Deontic Role that, if realized, is realized by its bearer's creating, revoking, or modifying some Deontic Role.

  • Duty Holder Role: A Deontic Role that inheres in an Agent A, that mutually depends on the existence of a Claimant Role borne by Agent B, and that specifies A performing or abstaining from some Act C, or providing or surrendering some Continuant D to B.

  • Privilege Holder Role: A Deontic Role that inheres in an Agent A, that specifies that no Agent B bears a Claimant Role against A performing Act C.

docs.title: Literature
docs.text:
Readings behind the Foundry's principles and patterns. Each page lists works with links to lawful copies where they exist. Suggestions are welcome through a pull request or Discussions.

Page Covers Adolf Reinach Social acts, claims and obligations, and the a priori foundations of law

More pages to come: basic formal ontology and document acts, Hohfeld and the theory of legal positions, and existing legal ontologies.

docs.title: Adolf Reinach
docs.text:
Adolf Reinach (1883 to 1917) gave the first systematic account of how claims, obligations, and other legal entities come into being through social acts such as promising, waiving, and enacting. His Apriori Foundations of the Civil Law (1913) anticipates speech act theory by half a century and supplies the philosophical core of several Foundry design patterns.

Links, not copies

The Foundry links to these works where they are lawfully available online. It hosts a text only when its rights holder has released it under an open license such as CC BY 4.0. To propose a link or a released text, see Contributing below.

docs.title: Reinach and the Foundry patterns
docs.text: Reinach Foundry pattern The social act (promise, waiver, enactment) that brings legal entities into being LOF-ODP-001: legal act establishing legal content The roles of promisor and promisee, and the persons who bear them LOF-ODP-002: legal role conferral Claim and obligation as correlative entities arising from a promise LOF-ODP-003: legal positions and their correlatives The dependence of enacted law on an act of enactment by someone with authority LOF-ODP-004: the Minimum Legal Chain

docs.title: Works by Reinach
docs.text:
The Apriori Foundations of the Civil Law

  • "Die apriorischen Grundlagen des bürgerlichen Rechtes," Jahrbuch für Philosophie und phänomenologische Forschung 1 (1913): 685 to 847.
  • English translation by John F. Crosby, Aletheia 3 (1983), with Crosby's biography of Reinach and his essay "Reinach's Discovery of the Social Acts." Stephan Kinsella describes the volume and links a scan at stephankinsella.com and on Mises Wire.
  • The Apriori Foundations of the Civil Law, Along with the Lecture "Concerning Phenomenology," trans. John F. Crosby (Frankfurt: Ontos, 2012; now De Gruyter).

Other writings

  • Über den Ursachenbegriff im geltenden Strafrecht (Leipzig: J. A. Barth, 1905), Reinach's dissertation. English: "On the Concept of Causality in the Criminal Law," trans. Berit Brogaard, Libertarian Papers 1, no. 35 (2009).
  • "Kant's Interpretation of Hume's Problem," trans. J. N. Mohanty, Southwestern Journal of Philosophy 7, no. 2 (1976): 161 to 188.
  • Sämtliche Werke: Textkritische Ausgabe in 2 Bänden, ed. Karl Schuhmann and Barry Smith (Munich: Philosophia, 1989).

docs.title: On Reinach
docs.text:
Overviews

  • "Adolf Reinach," Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, with a linked bibliography on PhilPapers.
  • Marietta Auer, Paul B. Miller, Henry E. Smith, and James Toomey, eds., Reinach and the Foundations of Private Law (Cambridge University Press, 2025; open access).

Social ontology and speech acts

  • Kevin Mulligan, ed., Speech Act and Sachverhalt: Reinach and the Foundations of Realist Phenomenology (Dordrecht: Nijhoff, 1987).
  • Barry Smith, "An Essay on Material Necessity," in Philip Hanson and Bruce Hunter, eds., Return of the A Priori, Canadian Journal of Philosophy Supplementary Volume 18 (1993): 301 to 322.
  • Barry Smith and Wojciech Żełaniec, "Laws of Essence or Constitutive Rules? Reinach vs. Searle on the Ontology of Social Entities," in Francesca De Vecchi, ed., Eidetica del Diritto e Ontologia Sociale: Il Realismo di Adolf Reinach (Milan: Mimesis, 2012): 83 to 108.
  • Kimberly Baltzer-Jaray, "Phenomenological Jurisprudence: A Reinterpretation of Adolf Reinach's Jahrbuch Essay," in J. Aaron Simmons and J. Edward Hackett, eds., Phenomenology for the Twenty-First Century (Palgrave Macmillan, 2016).

Causation, property, and Austrian law and economics

The Winter 2004 issue of the Quarterly Journal of Austrian Economics (vol. 7, no. 4) gathered papers on Reinach and the a priori foundations of law:

  • Stephan Kinsella and Patrick Tinsley, "Causation and Aggression," 97 to 112; revised in Kinsella, Legal Foundations of a Free Society (Houston: Papinian Press, 2023).
  • Hans-Hermann Hoppe, "Property, Causality, and Liability," 87 to 95; reprinted in Hoppe, The Great Fiction, 2nd ed. (Auburn, Ala.: Mises Institute, 2021).
  • Jörg Guido Hülsmann, "The A Priori Foundations of Property Economics," 41 to 68.
  • Larry J. Sechrest, "Praxeology, Economics, and Law: Issues and Implications," 19 to 40.
  • Walter Block, "Austrian Law and Economics: The Contributions of Adolf Reinach and Murray Rothbard," 69 to 85.
  • Leo Zaibert, "Toward Meta-Politics," 113 to 128.

Related:

  • Stephan Kinsella, "Causation, Aggression, the Law, and Reinach" (2004).
  • Stephan Kinsella, "Adolf Reinach and his 'On the Concept of Causality in the Criminal Law'," Kinsella on Liberty, episode 498.
  • Matt Mortellaro, "Causation and Responsibility: A New Direction," Libertarian Papers 1, no. 24 (2009).
  • Ben O'Neill and Walter Block, "Inchoate Crime, Accessories, and Constructive Malice in Libertarian Law," Libertarian Papers 5, no. 2 (2013): 241 to 271.

Forthcoming

  • Alessandro Fusillo, "Adolf Reinach and his 'A Priori Foundations of the Civil Law'."

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: To add a work, open a pull request that edits this page, or start a thread in Discussions. Give a full citation and a link to a lawful copy. To release your own work for the Foundry to host, say so in the request and confirm that you hold the rights.

docs.title: Design Patterns
docs.text:
Ontology design patterns (ODPs) are small, reusable modeling solutions to recurring problems in representing legal reality. Member ontologies are expected to use Foundry patterns where they apply, or to document why they depart from them (see principle LOF-P-004).

The first four patterns build on one another:

Pattern Title Depends on Status LOF-ODP-001 Legal Act and Legal Document BFO draft LOF-ODP-002 Legal Role Conferral ODP-001 draft LOF-ODP-003 Correlative Deontic Positions ODP-001 draft, placement decision open LOF-ODP-004 Minimum Legal Chain ODP-001, 002, 003 draft, placement-neutral

A worked example, a residential lease, runs through all four.

New patterns follow the pattern template.

docs.title: LOF-ODP-001: Legal Act and Legal Document
docs.text:
Identifier LOF-ODP-001 IRI https://w3id.org/lof/odp-001.owl Repository https://github.com/legal-ontologies-foundry/lof-odp-001 Status draft Version 0.1.0 Drafted by David R. Koepsell For review by William Mandrick, Barry Smith

Draft for review

First draft, prepared for discussion by the founding coordinators. Open questions are listed at the end.

docs.title: Intent
docs.text: Legal information systems routinely use one word for three different things. "The lease" may mean the signing that took place on 1 March, the terms the parties agreed to, or the stapled pages in a drawer. These differ in kind: the signing is over, the terms persist, and the pages can be burned without the terms ceasing to bind. This pattern separates the legal act, the legal content it establishes, and the legal documents that carry that content, so that every other Foundry pattern can refer to them unambiguously.

docs.title: Competency questions
docs.text:
1. Which legal act established this legal content, and when?
  2. Which persons or organizations participated in that act?
  3. Under what pre-existing legal content (an enabling statute, a procedural rule) was the act performed?
  4. Which documents carry this legal content?
  5. Do these two documents carry the same legal content?

docs.title: Classes
docs.text: Label IRI BFO parent Definition legal act ODP001_0001000 process A process, having one or more persons or organizations as participants, that a legal system recognizes as bringing into being, modifying, or terminating legally significant entities. legal content ODP001_0001001 generically dependent continuant A generically dependent continuant that is established by some legal act and that specifies legally significant entities, such as the provisions of a statute, the terms of a contract, or the holding of a judgment. legal document ODP001_0001002 material entity A material entity that is the carrier of some legal content. enactment ODP001_0001003 legal act A legal act in which a body with legislative authority establishes legal content of general application. contract formation ODP001_0001004 legal act A legal act in which two or more parties establish legal content that binds them to one another.

docs.title: Relations
docs.text:
Label IRI Domain Range Definition establishes ODP001_0001100 legal act legal content A relation between a legal act and the legal content that comes into being through that act. established by ODP001_0001101 legal content legal act Inverse of establishes. performed under ODP001_0001102 legal act legal content A relation between a legal act and pre-existing legal content that authorizes or governs it.

The pattern reuses BFO has participant (BFO:0000057) for the parties to an act and BFO is carrier of (BFO:0000101) between a document and its content.

docs.title: Axioms (Manchester syntax)
docs.text:
legal act       SubClassOf  process and (has participant some material entity)
legal content   SubClassOf  generically dependent continuant
legal document  SubClassOf  material entity and (is carrier of some legal content)
enactment          SubClassOf  legal act and (establishes some legal content)
contract formation SubClassOf  legal act and (establishes some legal content)
enactment DisjointWith contract formation

docs.title: Grounding rationale (LOF-P-004)
docs.text:
• Legal act as process. A signing, a vote, or the delivery of a judgment unfolds in time and has temporal parts. It is over once it is complete, while what it brings about persists.
  • Legal content as generically dependent continuant. The same statute exists in the official gazette, in every printed code, and on every server that stores it, and it survives the destruction of any one copy. That is the defining feature of a generically dependent continuant.
  • Legal document as material entity. The particular signed paper, or the particular stored file, is a material thing that carries the content. Digital documents are treated as patterns in material storage media.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The signing of a residential lease (hypothetical parties):

ex:leaseSigning a odp1:0001004 ;          # contract formation
    obo:BFO_0000057 ex:ana , ex:northside ;   # has participant
    odp1:0001100 ex:leaseTerms ;              # establishes
    odp1:0001102 ex:tenantCode .              # performed under

ex:leaseTerms a odp1:0001001 .               # legal content

ex:copyHeldByAna       a odp1:0001002 ; obo:BFO_0000101 ex:leaseTerms .
ex:copyHeldByNorthside a odp1:0001002 ; obo:BFO_0000101 ex:leaseTerms .

The two copies are distinct material entities carrying one and the same legal content. The full example is in lof-odp-003/src/examples/lease-example.ttl.

docs.title: Alignment with legal standards (LOF-P-015)
docs.text: This pattern Akoma Ntoso / ELI (FRBR-derived) IAO legal content Work and Expression levels information content entity (IAO:0000030), close match legal document Item level none. IAO document (IAO:0000310) is an information content entity, and so corresponds to legal content legal act lifecycle events none

docs.title: Consequences and limitations
docs.text:
• The pattern does not distinguish versions of legal content (an amended statute versus the original). The FRBR Work and Expression distinction collapses here into a single class, which is a deliberate simplification for a first pattern.
  • Legal act requires at least one participant. Acts by operation of law with no human participant, if there are any, fall outside it.
  • Enactment and contract formation are illustrative subclasses. Domain ontologies will add many more (adjudication, conveyance, delegation).

docs.title: Open questions for the founding coordinators
docs.text:
1. Should the Foundry import IAO and place legal content under IAO information content entity, rather than directly under generically dependent continuant with a mapping? Importing IAO increases interoperability with OBO, at the cost of an extra dependency.
  2. Should the Work and Expression distinction be modeled in this pattern, or deferred to a later versioning pattern?
  3. Is the treatment of digital documents as patterns in material media acceptable, or does it need a pattern of its own?

docs.title: Related patterns
docs.text:
• LOF-ODP-002 uses legal act for role conferral and termination.
  • LOF-ODP-003 grounds legal positions in legal content, and relates powers to the legal acts in which they are exercised.

docs.title: LOF-ODP-002: Legal Role Conferral
docs.text:
Identifier LOF-ODP-002 IRI https://w3id.org/lof/odp-002.owl Repository https://github.com/legal-ontologies-foundry/lof-odp-002 Status draft Version 0.1.0 Depends on LOF-ODP-001 Drafted by David R. Koepsell For review by William Mandrick, Barry Smith

Draft for review

First draft, prepared for discussion by the founding coordinators. Open questions are listed at the end.

docs.title: Intent
docs.text: A great deal of law is about who occupies which legal role: judge, trustee, executor, guardian, tenant, director. Roles are acquired and lost through legal acts (appointments, contracts, removals, resignations), and they are specified by legal content (the statute creating an office, the lease clause defining the tenant's position). This pattern models legal roles as BFO roles and connects them to the acts that confer and terminate them, and to the content that specifies them.

docs.title: Competency questions
docs.text:
1. Which legal roles does this person or organization currently bear?
  2. Which legal act conferred this role, and under what legal content?
  3. Which legal act terminated this role?
  4. Which legal content specifies what this role consists in?
  5. Which of a person's legal roles arose by operation of law rather than by a conferring act?

docs.title: Classes
docs.text: Label IRI BFO parent Definition legal role ODP002_0001000 role A role that inheres in a person or organization in virtue of some legal act or legal content, and that is realized in processes having legal significance. conferred legal role ODP002_0001001 legal role (defined) A legal role that was brought into existence by some legal act. role conferral act ODP002_0001002 legal act (defined) A legal act that brings some legal role into existence in some bearer. role termination act ODP002_0001003 legal act (defined) A legal act that brings some legal role to an end.

docs.title: Relations
docs.text:
Label IRI Domain Range Definition confers ODP002_0001100 legal act legal role A relation between a legal act and a legal role that comes into existence through that act. conferred by ODP002_0001101 legal role legal act Inverse of confers. terminates ODP002_0001102 legal act legal role A relation between a legal act and a legal role that ceases to exist through that act. specified by ODP002_0001103 legal role legal content A relation between a legal role and legal content that specifies what the role consists in.

The pattern reuses BFO inheres in (BFO:0000197) between a role and its bearer, and BFO realizes (BFO:0000055) between a process and the role it realizes.

docs.title: Axioms (Manchester syntax)
docs.text:
legal role  SubClassOf  role and (inheres in some material entity)
conferred legal role  EquivalentTo  legal role and (conferred by some legal act)
role conferral act    EquivalentTo  legal act and (confers some legal role)
role termination act  EquivalentTo  legal act and (terminates some legal role)

The last three are defined classes, so the reasoner classifies instances automatically. In the worked example, the lease signing is asserted only to be a contract formation that confers a tenant role; the reasoner infers that it is a role conferral act, and that the tenant role is a conferred legal role.

docs.title: Grounding rationale (LOF-P-004)
docs.text: A person becomes a trustee, or ceases to be one, without any change in their physical make-up. The role exists because of external circumstances (an instrument, an appointment, a court order). That is the defining feature of a BFO role, as opposed to a disposition, which is grounded in the bearer's physical make-up.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
ex:anaTenantRole a odp2:0001000 ;        # legal role
    obo:BFO_0000197 ex:ana ;             # inheres in
    odp2:0001101 ex:leaseSigning ;       # conferred by
    odp2:0001103 ex:leaseTerms .         # specified by

Inferred: ex:anaTenantRole is a conferred legal role; ex:leaseSigning is a role conferral act.

docs.title: Alignment with legal standards (LOF-P-015)
docs.text: Compatible with role modeling in the Common Core Ontologies and with the agent-role distinction in LKIF-Core, but grounded directly in BFO role. Akoma Ntoso's TLCRole and TLCPerson references can be mapped to legal role and its bearer.

docs.title: Consequences and limitations
docs.text:
• Roles arising by operation of law (a parent's guardianship of a newborn) are legal roles but not conferred legal roles. The pattern does not yet model what brings them into existence.
  • The pattern does not state that the bearer of a conferred role participates in the conferring act. That is often true (a signing) and sometimes false (an appointment by letter), so it is left to domain ontologies.
  • Offices that persist through changes of holder (the office of Chief Justice, as opposed to a particular person's role as Chief Justice) are not modeled. This is the most significant gap.

docs.title: Open questions for the founding coordinators
docs.text:
1. Offices. Should the Foundry model an office as something distinct from the roles of its successive holders? If so, is an office a generically dependent continuant specified by legal content, of which each holder's role is a concretization?
  2. Should legal role be required to be specified by some legal content, making the link to the law mandatory rather than optional?
  3. How should roles borne by organizations be treated, given that BFO has no settled account of organizations?

docs.title: Related patterns
docs.text:
• LOF-ODP-001 supplies legal act and legal content.
  • LOF-ODP-003: the power to confer a role is a second-order legal position, exercised in a role conferral act.

docs.title: LOF-ODP-003: Correlative Deontic Positions
docs.text:
Identifier LOF-ODP-003 IRI https://w3id.org/lof/odp-003.owl Repository https://github.com/legal-ontologies-foundry/lof-odp-003 Status draft, with an open placement decision Version 0.1.0 Depends on LOF-ODP-001 Drafted by David R. Koepsell For review by William Mandrick, Barry Smith

Decision required

This pattern is published in two versions that differ only in the BFO placement of legal position. The founding coordinators are asked to choose between them. See the decision.

docs.title: Intent
docs.text:
Wesley Hohfeld showed that the word "right" covers four different legal positions, each paired with a correlative held by another party:

Position Correlative Order claim duty first-order: what parties must or may do liberty no-claim first-order power liability second-order: who can change first-order positions immunity disability second-order

This pattern models the eight positions, their correlative pairing, their holders, the legal content that grounds them, and the legal acts in which powers are exercised. It gives every Foundry ontology a common vocabulary for rights and duties that is more precise than the word "right" alone.

docs.title: Competency questions
docs.text:
1. What duties does this person hold, and to whom are they owed?
  2. What is the correlative of this claim, and who holds it?
  3. In virtue of what legal content does this position exist?
  4. Which legal acts were exercises of this power?
  5. Does this position survive the assignment of the claim, or the death of its holder?

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
Label IRI Parent Correlative legal position ODP003_0001000 see decision first-order legal position ODP003_0001009 legal position second-order legal position ODP003_0001010 legal position claim (alt. right) ODP003_0001001 first-order duty duty ODP003_0001002 first-order claim liberty (alt. privilege) ODP003_0001003 first-order no-claim no-claim (alt. no-right) ODP003_0001004 first-order liberty power ODP003_0001005 second-order liability liability ODP003_0001006 second-order power immunity ODP003_0001007 second-order disability disability ODP003_0001008 second-order immunity

Definitions for all eleven classes are in the ontology file. For example, duty: "A first-order legal position in virtue of which its holder is required to engage in, or refrain from, some conduct owed to another party."

docs.title: Relations
docs.text: Label IRI Definition held by ODP003_0001100 A relation between a legal position and the person or organization whose position it is. grounded in ODP003_0001101 A relation between a legal position and the legal content in virtue of which it exists. correlative of ODP003_0001102 A symmetric relation between two legal positions held by different parties, each of which exists if and only if the other does. exercised in ODP003_0001103 A relation between a power and a legal act through which the holder changes the legal positions of another party.

docs.title: Axioms (Manchester syntax, common to both options)
docs.text:
legal position SubClassOf (held by some material entity)
                      and (grounded in some legal content)
                      and (correlative of some legal position)
claim SubClassOf  first-order legal position
            and (correlative of some duty) and (correlative of only duty)
duty  SubClassOf  first-order legal position
            and (correlative of some claim) and (correlative of only claim)
... likewise for the other three pairs ...
DisjointClasses: claim, duty, liberty, no-claim, power, liability, immunity, disability
correlative of: Symmetric

docs.title: The placement decision
docs.text:
The two options differ in two axioms only.

Option A (editors' file) Option B (alternatives/) legal position SubClassOf specifically dependent continuant (BFO:0000020) generically dependent continuant (BFO:0000031) held by functional subproperty of BFO inheres in ordinary relation, not functional A position is... a feature of its holder, like a role a piece of legal content's upshot, related to a holder Can a position change holders? No. It ends when its holder ceases to hold it. Yes. The same position can pass to a new holder. Assignment of a claim the old claim ends; a new claim begins in the assignee the same claim is now held by the assignee Death of a debtor the duty ends; the estate bears a new duty the same duty passes to the estate Fit with ODP-002 uniform: roles and positions both inhere in bearers positions and roles are of different kinds Fit with ODP-001 positions are distinct from the content grounding them positions are close in kind to legal content

Held by is functional in Option A because BFO's axioms state that a specifically dependent continuant has exactly one bearer. BFO's OWL file does not encode this, so the pattern states it explicitly.

docs.title: A test that separates them
docs.text:
The repository includes a worked example (a residential lease) and an assignment test, in which the landlord assigns its claim to rent to a collection agency, and the agency is said to hold the same claim. make test-options reasons over both:

Lease example Same claim after assignment Option A consistent inconsistent Option B consistent consistent

So the choice is not merely metaphysical. It determines how every Foundry ontology must represent assignment, succession, subrogation, and novation. Under Option A, these are all modeled as the ending of one position and the beginning of another, linked by a legal act. Under Option B, they are changes in the holder of a single persisting position.

docs.title: Considerations
docs.text:
For Option A. It treats legal positions uniformly with legal roles (ODP-002). It keeps a clear line between the content of the law, which is generically dependent, and what the law brings about in particular persons, which is specifically dependent. It also matches ordinary legal talk of a person having a duty in the way they have a role. Novation, where a new obligation replaces the old, fits it naturally.

For Option B. Legal practice often treats a claim as a transferable asset, the same claim passing from assignor to assignee. Option B represents that directly, without multiplying positions. It also aligns with approaches that treat obligations as directive information content, such as the Common Core Ontologies' directive information content entities.

Declaration of interest. The drafter's own work (A Structural Ontology of the Law) treats obligations as specifically dependent continuants, as in Option A. Option A is placed in the editors' file only so that the pattern has a working default; it carries no presumption.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
ex:anaRentDuty a odp3:0001002 ;            # duty
    odp3:0001100 ex:ana ;                  # held by
    odp3:0001101 ex:leaseTerms ;           # grounded in
    odp3:0001102 ex:northsideRentClaim .   # correlative of

ex:northsideRentClaim a odp3:0001001 ;     # claim
    odp3:0001100 ex:northside ;
    odp3:0001101 ex:leaseTerms .

ex:northsideTerminationPower a odp3:0001005 ;   # power
    odp3:0001100 ex:northside ;
    odp3:0001101 ex:tenantCode ;
    odp3:0001102 ex:anaTerminationLiability .

docs.title: Alignment with legal standards (LOF-P-015)
docs.text: The eight positions follow Hohfeld's Fundamental Legal Conceptions (1913, 1917). LKIF-Core and LegalRuleML represent obligations and permissions as deontic modalities or rule components, rather than as entities with holders, so their mapping to this pattern is partial. It will be documented once the placement question is settled.

docs.title: Consequences and limitations
docs.text:
• The pattern does not say what a position is about: the action type a duty requires (paying rent) or a liberty permits. Referring to types of action is a known difficulty in OWL; the options are listed below.
  • OWL cannot express that correlatives are held by different parties, or that a claim and its correlative duty concern the same action. These are documented constraints, not enforced ones.
  • Hohfeld's jural opposites (claim versus no-claim in the same holder) are not modeled, because they relate a position to the absence of another.

docs.title: Open questions for the founding coordinators
docs.text:
1. Placement. Option A or Option B? (The central question.)
  2. Action types. How should a position indicate the conduct it concerns? Options: (a) a relation to a plan specification or directive information content entity, following IAO and CCO; (b) a relation to a process universal via OWL punning; (c) a relation to a process profile. Each has costs for reasoning.
  3. Realizability. Should duties, liberties, and powers be treated as realizable entities, realized in compliance, in acting, and in the exercise of the power? This is available only under Option A.
  4. Should correlatives be modeled as parts of a single relational whole (a legal relation between two parties), rather than as two linked positions?

docs.title: Related patterns
docs.text:
• LOF-ODP-001 supplies legal content (grounding) and legal act (exercise of powers).
  • LOF-ODP-002: conferring a legal role is typically the exercise of a power, and a role is typically specified by the positions its holder acquires.

docs.title: LOF-ODP-004: Minimum Legal Chain
docs.text:
Identifier LOF-ODP-004 IRI https://w3id.org/lof/odp-004.owl Repository https://github.com/legal-ontologies-foundry/lof-odp-004 Status draft Version 0.1.0 Depends on LOF-ODP-001, LOF-ODP-002, LOF-ODP-003 Drafted by David R. Koepsell For review by William Mandrick, Barry Smith

Draft for review

First draft, prepared for discussion by the founding coordinators. Open questions are listed at the end.

docs.title: Intent
docs.text:
The first three patterns say what legal acts, legal content, legal roles, and legal positions are. They do not say how these fit together when a particular duty or claim comes to exist. A tenant's duty to pay April rent exists because a power to contract was exercised in a signing, which established lease terms, under which the start of April is a triggering occurrence, producing a duty owed to the landlord, backed by a remedy if it is not discharged. Remove any one of these and the duty is either absent or defective.

This pattern connects the eight links of that chain (authority, norm, actor in role, trigger, act, target, effect, remedy) using the classes of ODP-001 to ODP-003, adds the few relations they lack, and defines a class for positions whose chain is complete. A companion set of SHACL shapes reports, node by node, where a chain is incomplete.

docs.title: Competency questions
docs.text:
1. Under what power, exercised in what act, was the legal content grounding this position established?
  2. What occurrence triggered this position, and through what act or occurrence did it come into existence?
  3. At whom or what is this position directed?
  4. What legal content provides a remedy if this position is not discharged?
  5. Which positions were not discharged, during what period, and what remedial positions arose in consequence?
  6. Which positions are fully grounded, and at which link does each incomplete chain fail?

Questions 1 to 5 are answered by SPARQL (src/sparql/); question 6 by the defined class and the SHACL shapes (src/shapes/).

docs.title: The chain
docs.text: Node Cluster Occupied by From 1 Source of authority AUTHORITY norm-establishing power ODP-003 power (defined here) 2 Norm AUTHORITY legal content ODP-001 3 Actor in role AUTHORITY legal role, realized in the generating act ODP-002 4 Triggering facts EFFECT triggering occurrence new (defined) 5 Legal act or omission EFFECT legal act; omission via undischarged during ODP-001; new relation 6 Target RECOGNITION whatever the position is directed at new relation 7 Legal effect RECOGNITION legal position ODP-003 8 Remedy REPAIR remedial position; remedy provided by new (defined); new relation

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
Label IRI BFO parent Definition norm-establishing power ODP004_0001000 power (defined) A power that is exercised in some legal act that establishes legal content. triggering occurrence ODP004_0001001 occurrent (defined) An occurrent that satisfies a condition, set out in legal content, for some legal position to come into existence. remedial position ODP004_0001002 legal position (defined) A legal position that exists because some other legal position was not discharged, and whose discharge or exercise is directed to making good that failure. fully grounded legal position ODP004_0001003 legal position (defined) A legal position that is grounded in legal content established by a legal act in which some power was exercised, that is triggered by some occurrent, that is generated by a legal act realizing some legal role, that is directed at some entity, and for whose non-discharge some legal content provides a remedy.

All four are defined classes. The pattern introduces no new primitive categories: every entity in a chain is already an ODP-001 to ODP-003 entity or a BFO occurrent.

docs.title: Relations
docs.text:
Label IRI Domain Range Definition generated by ODP004_0001100 legal position occurrent A relation between a legal position and an occurrent through which the position comes into existence. generates ODP004_0001101 occurrent legal position Inverse of generated by. triggered by ODP004_0001102 legal position occurrent A relation between a legal position and an occurrent that satisfies a condition, set out in the legal content in which the position is grounded, for the position to come into existence. directed at ODP004_0001103 legal position entity A relation between a legal position and an entity toward which the position is oriented, either the holder of its correlative position or a thing over which the position obtains. remedies ODP004_0001104 legal position legal position A relation between a legal position and another legal position, whose non-discharge is the occasion of the first and whose discharge or exercise is directed to making good that non-discharge. remedy provided by ODP004_0001105 legal position legal content A relation between a legal position and legal content that specifies which remedial positions arise if the position is not discharged. undischarged during ODP004_0001106 first-order legal position temporal region A relation between a first-order legal position and a temporal region during which no process occurs that complies with the position.

The pattern reuses BFO realizes (BFO:0000055) between the generating act and the actor's legal role.

docs.title: Axioms (Manchester syntax)
docs.text:
norm-establishing power  EquivalentTo  power
    and (exercised in some (legal act and (establishes some legal content)))
triggering occurrence    EquivalentTo  occurrent and (inverse (triggered by) some legal position)
remedial position        EquivalentTo  legal position and (remedies some legal position)

fully grounded legal position  EquivalentTo  legal position
    and (grounded in some (legal content
          and (established by some (legal act and (inverse (exercised in) some power)))))
    and (triggered by some occurrent)
    and (generated by some (legal act and (realizes some legal role)))
    and (directed at some entity)
    and (remedy provided by some legal content)

correlative of o held by  SubPropertyOf  directed at

The property chain means that party targets are never asserted: a duty whose correlative claim is held by the landlord is inferred to be directed at the landlord. Thing targets (land, a patented invention, a data set) are asserted directly.

docs.title: Grounding rationale (LOF-P-004)
docs.text:
• Norm-establishing power, remedial position, fully grounded legal position. These are defined subclasses of ODP-003 classes. Their BFO category is whatever the ODP-003 placement decision makes it. This pattern takes no position on that decision, and the repository tests it under both options (see below).
  • Triggering occurrence as occurrent. What the law treats as operative is a change: a signing, a death, the start or end of a period. Where a statute speaks of a standing state ("a person who is eighteen"), the operative occurrence is the process boundary at which the state begins. Occurrent, rather than process, is the parent because the end of a period (a temporal instant) is among the most common triggers.
  • Omission without negative occurrents. BFO has no category for events that did not happen. The pattern therefore does not reify omissions. It asserts that a position went undischarged during a temporal region, and treats the end of that region as the triggering occurrence of any remedial position.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Continuing the residential lease, with the chain for April rent:

ex:anaContractPower a odp3:0001005 ;        # power
    odp3:0001100 ex:ana ;                   # held by
    odp3:0001101 ex:tenantCode ;            # grounded in
    odp3:0001103 ex:leaseSigning .          # exercised in           (node 1)

ex:leaseSigning a odp1:0001004 ;            # contract formation     (node 5)
    odp1:0001100 ex:leaseTerms ;            # establishes            (node 2)
    obo:BFO_0000055 ex:anaPartyRole .       # realizes               (node 3)

ex:anaAprilRentDuty a odp3:0001002 ;        # duty                   (node 7)
    odp3:0001100 ex:ana ;
    odp3:0001101 ex:leaseTerms ;
    odp3:0001102 ex:northsideAprilRentClaim ;
    odp4:0001102 ex:aprilPeriodStart ;      # triggered by           (node 4)
    odp4:0001100 ex:leaseSigning ;          # generated by
    odp4:0001105 ex:tenantCode .            # remedy provided by     (node 8)

ex:anaAprilRentDuty odp4:0001106 ex:aprilPaymentWindow .   # undischarged during

ex:northsideLateFeeClaim a odp3:0001001 ;   # claim
    odp4:0001104 ex:anaAprilRentDuty ;      # remedies
    odp4:0001102 ex:aprilWindowEnd ;        # triggered by
    odp4:0001100 ex:aprilWindowEnd .        # generated by (operation of law)

Inferred by HermiT, under both ODP-003 options: the rent duty is a fully grounded legal position directed at Northside; the late-fee claim is a remedial position; Ana's contracting power is a norm-establishing power; the start of April and the end of 5 April are triggering occurrences.

The example also contains a defective chain: an oral side promise to repaint, with no trigger, no generating act, and no remedy. It is not classified as fully grounded, and the SHACL report locates the failure:

Position Node 1 Node 3 Node 4 Node 5 Node 6 Node 8 duty to pay April rent ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ (inferred) ✓ claim to a late fee ✓ warning ✓ ✓ ✓ (inferred) ✓ duty to repaint violation warning violation violation ✓ (inferred) violation

The warning at node 3 on the late fee is the operation-of-law case (open question 2). The full example is src/examples/lease-chain.ttl.

docs.title: Alignment with legal standards (LOF-P-015)
docs.text:
This pattern LegalRuleML LKIF-Core Akoma Ntoso triggering occurrence antecedent of a prescriptive statement (conditions), close match at the type level none eventRef for lifecycle events, partial remedial position, remedies reparation statement linking an obligation to a penalty, close match none none legal position deontic formulas (obligation, permission), partial as in ODP-003 normatively qualified entities, partial none norm-establishing power authority metadata, partial legal power, close match TLCOrganization as author of the act, partial

LegalRuleML represents these as parts of rules, that is, at the type level. This pattern represents them at the instance level, as the particular chain behind a particular duty. The two are complementary: a LegalRuleML rule states the conditions, and an ODP-004 chain records that they were met.

docs.title: Consequences and limitations
docs.text:
• Instance level only. The pattern relates a particular position to the particular trigger and act behind it. It does not say which types of occurrence trigger which types of position. That is the same action-type problem as ODP-003 open question 2, and should be solved once for both.
  • Open world. OWL can classify a complete chain but cannot infer that a chain is incomplete, since a missing link may simply be unrecorded. Incompleteness is reported by the SHACL shapes, which should be run on a reasoned graph.
  • No temporal ordering. Nothing requires the trigger to precede the position, or the grounding content to predate the act. Temporal constraints are left to domain ontologies.
  • Correlative sharing. The shapes accept a link recorded on either member of a correlative pair, so the chain need only be recorded once per legal relation.
  • Placement-neutral. make test-options reasons over the example with both ODP-003 options. Both are consistent and yield identical classifications, so adopting this pattern does not prejudge the ODP-003 decision.

docs.title: Relation to A Structural Ontology of the Law
docs.text:
The eight-node chain is the Minimum Legal Chain of Koepsell, A Structural Ontology of the Law (Palgrave Macmillan, forthcoming), where it underlies a typology of legal contradictions indexed to the links of the chain and a measure of structural instability built on that typology. Only the chain is proposed here. The typology and the measure are theory-specific and are deliberately left out, consistent with LOF-P-008 and LOF-P-009. The node-labeled SHACL report is the point of contact: any diagnostic ontology, SOoL's or another, can consume it without being part of this pattern.

Declaration of interest. The drafter is the author of that book.

docs.title: Open questions for the founding coordinators
docs.text:
1. Is chain closure a Foundry commitment? Fully grounded legal position builds in two substantive claims: that a legal position requires a remedy (ubi jus ibi remedium), and that it requires an actor in role. Should the Foundry define this class, or publish only the relations and leave closure to the SHACL shapes?
  2. Operation of law. Positions arising without any act (the late fee, intestate succession, a newborn's guardian) fail node 3. Should node 3 accept any generating occurrent, should such positions trace their actor to the enactment of the grounding content, or should they be a documented exception? This is also ODP-002's gap for roles arising by operation of law.
  3. Omission. Is undischarged during acceptable, or should omission be modeled as the non-realization of a realizable entity? The second is available only under ODP-003 Option A.
  4. Remedial regress. The shapes require remedial positions to have remedy provisions of their own. Should there be a terminal category (enforcement by the state) that closes the regress?
  5. Thing targets. Positions directed at things rather than persons (property, in rem rights) are supported but not modeled. Do they need their own pattern?

docs.text:
• LOF-ODP-001 supplies legal act (node 5) and legal content (node 2).
  • LOF-ODP-002 supplies legal role (node 3).
  • LOF-ODP-003 supplies legal position (node 7), power (node 1), and correlative of, from which targets (node 6) are inferred.

docs.title: Deprecation policy
docs.text: Terms are never deleted (LOF-P-005). A term that should no longer be used is deprecated, following the same conventions as the OBO Foundry's obsoletion policy.

docs.title: When to deprecate
docs.text:
• The term's meaning must change. Deprecate it and mint a new term.
  • The term duplicates another term, in this or another member ontology (LOF-P-009).
  • The term was created in error, or is out of scope.

Changes to a label or a definition that do not change the term's meaning do not require deprecation.

docs.title: How to deprecate
docs.text:
1. Add owl:deprecated true.
  2. Prefix the label with obsolete (for example, "obsolete legal duty").
  3. Remove all logical axioms in which the term appears (subclass axioms, equivalences, restrictions), so it no longer affects reasoning.
  4. Add one of the following:
    • IAO:0100001 (term replaced by) pointing to the single replacement term, or
    • oboInOwl:consider pointing to one or more candidate terms, when there is no exact replacement.
  5. Add an rdfs:comment explaining why, with a link to the issue.
  6. Record the deprecation in CHANGELOG.md.

The automated check deprecated-without-replacement-violation enforces step 4.

docs.title: Deprecating an ontology
docs.text: An ontology that is no longer maintained or has been superseded is set to status: deprecated in the registry, with replaced_by naming its successor if there is one. Its identifiers and releases remain resolvable indefinitely.

docs.title: ID ranges
docs.text: To stop two editors from minting the same identifier, each editor of an ontology is allocated a range of seven-digit numbers. Allocations are recorded in src/ontology/lof-{id}-idranges.owl in the ontology's repository, in the format used by the OBO Foundry and the Ontology Development Kit.

docs.title: Default allocation
docs.text: Range Use 0000001 to 0000999 Reserved 0001000 to 0001999 First editor 0002000 to 0002999 Second editor 0003000 to 0003999 Third editor 0004000 and above Allocated on request

docs.title: Protégé setup
docs.text:
In Protégé, open Preferences > New Entities and set:

  • Entity IRI: Start with Specified IRI https://w3id.org/lof, Followed by /, End with Auto-generated ID.
  • Entity Label: Custom label, rdfs:label.
  • Auto-generated ID: Numeric (iterative), prefix {PREFIX}_, 7 digits, starting at the beginning of your range, and ending at its end.

To request a range, open an issue in the ontology's repository, or ask its contact person.

docs.title: Identifier policy
docs.text: All Foundry identifiers live in the persistent namespace https://w3id.org/lof/. The redirects are maintained in the w3id.org repository and generated from the registry, so hosting can change without breaking any identifier (LOF-P-005).

docs.title: Patterns
docs.text:
Kind Pattern Example Foundry home https://w3id.org/lof/ Full release (latest) https://w3id.org/lof/{id}.owl https://w3id.org/lof/odp-001.owl Base release (latest) https://w3id.org/lof/{id}/{id}-base.owl https://w3id.org/lof/odp-001/odp-001-base.owl Specific release https://w3id.org/lof/{id}/releases/{version}/{id}.owl https://w3id.org/lof/odp-001/releases/0.1.0/odp-001.owl Import module https://w3id.org/lof/{id}/imports/{file} https://w3id.org/lof/odp-001/imports/bfo_import.owl Term https://w3id.org/lof/{PREFIX}_{7 digits} https://w3id.org/lof/ODP001_0001000 Issue tracker https://w3id.org/lof/{id}/tracker Home page https://w3id.org/lof/{id}/home

{id} is the lower-case registry identifier. {PREFIX} is the upper-case prefix reserved in the registry.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
1. Local identifiers are opaque seven-digit numbers. They never encode labels.
  2. An identifier, once published in a release, is never reassigned and never deleted. See the deprecation policy.
  3. Each editor mints identifiers only from their allocated ID range.
  4. Prefixes are reserved when an ontology is registered at draft status and remain reserved even if it is deprecated.

docs.title: Term resolution
docs.text: Term IRIs currently redirect to the ontology's page in the registry. When a term browser is deployed (for example, an OLS or Ontobee instance), the term redirects will be updated to point at it, with no change to the IRIs.

docs.title: Registry metadata
docs.text:
Each ontology in the registry is described by one file, ontology/{id}.md, in the website repository. The file has YAML front matter holding the metadata, followed by a Markdown body holding a longer description. This is the same arrangement the OBO Foundry uses.

The front matter is validated against the JSON Schema in util/schema/registry_schema.json on every pull request. From these files the build generates:

  • the registry page and one page per ontology,
  • machine-readable registries at registry/ontologies.yml and registry/ontologies.jsonld,
  • the .htaccess redirects for w3id.org/lof.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text: Field Required Meaning id yes Lower-case identifier; must match the file name. preferred_prefix yes Upper-case prefix for term IRIs. title yes Full title. description yes One-sentence description. domain yes The part of legal reality covered. jurisdictions yes Jurisdictions or traditions in scope, or general (LOF-P-010). status yes draft, candidate, accepted, or deprecated. activity_status yes active, inactive, or orphaned. repository yes GitHub repository URL. tracker yes Issue tracker URL. license yes label and url. contact yes label, email, and github (LOF-P-017). homepage no Defaults to the repository. branch no Release branch; defaults to main. dependencies no List of ids: registry ids or bfo, ro, iao, cco. usages no List of description and optional url (LOF-P-016). publications no List of id (DOI or URL) and title. review no date and issue URL of the review that set the status. replaced_by no For deprecated ontologies, the successor's id.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: status Meaning draft Registered and under development. The prefix is reserved. candidate Submitted for review against the principles. accepted Reviewed and found to satisfy the principles. deprecated Superseded or no longer maintained. Identifiers remain resolvable. activity_status Meaning active Maintainers are responsive and releases are current. inactive No release or issue activity for 12 months. orphaned Maintainers have withdrawn; new maintainers sought.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
Draft for ratification

These principles are a founding draft, modeled on the OBO Foundry principles and adapted to the legal domain. They take effect when ratified by the founding coordinators under the rules in Governance.

Every member ontology commits to the following principles. Each has its own page setting out its purpose, requirements, implementation, and the criteria reviewers apply. Principle numbers are permanent and never reused, so reviews and discussions can cite them precisely (for example, "fails LOF-P-007").

Principles LOF-P-004 (explicit grounding of legal entities) and LOF-P-010 (jurisdictional transparency) have no direct OBO counterpart. They address problems specific to law.

ID Principle Summary LOF-P-001 Open The ontology is openly available and may be used by all without constraint other than attribution. LOF-P-002 Common format The ontology is released in OWL 2, with a stable primary release file. LOF-P-003 Common upper ontology The ontology is aligned to Basic Formal Ontology, and every class descends from a BFO class. LOF-P-004 Explicit grounding of legal entities Each top-level legal class states which BFO category it falls under, and why. LOF-P-005 Persistent identifiers Every entity has a persistent IRI in the https://w3id.org/lof/ namespace, and IRIs are never reassigned or deleted. LOF-P-006 Versioning Each release carries a version IRI and version number, and every earlier release remains resolvable. LOF-P-007 Textual definitions Every class and relation has a precise, non-circular textual definition. LOF-P-008 Clearly delineated scope The ontology has a stated scope and a set of competency questions. LOF-P-009 Orthogonality Member ontologies do not duplicate one another's content. LOF-P-010 Jurisdictional transparency Classes specific to a legal system or jurisdiction are marked as such and are not presented as universal. LOF-P-011 Logical well-formedness Each release is logically consistent and contains no unsatisfiable classes. LOF-P-012 Naming conventions Labels are unique, singular, and follow a consistent lexical style. LOF-P-013 Documentation The ontology has a public repository with documentation and an issue tracker. LOF-P-014 Responsiveness and maintenance Maintainers respond to issues and keep the ontology aligned with its dependencies. LOF-P-015 Alignment with existing legal standards The ontology documents its relationship to established legal information standards. LOF-P-016 Documented use The ontology has documented users, or a credible plan for use. LOF-P-017 Locus of authority Each ontology has a single named point of contact responsible for it. LOF-P-018 Attribution Contributors to the ontology are credited, and it can be cited.

Checks that can be automated are listed on the automated checks page.

docs.title: LOF-P-001: Open
docs.text:
Draft for ratification

Part of the founding draft of the LOF principles.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The ontology is openly available and may be used by all without constraint other than attribution.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Legal ontologies are infrastructure for courts, agencies, researchers, and developers across jurisdictions. Restrictive licenses fragment that infrastructure and prevent the integration the Foundry exists to support.

docs.title: Recommendations and requirements
docs.text:
1. The ontology is released under CC BY 4.0 or CC0 1.0.
  2. The license is declared in the ontology header with dcterms:license whose value is the license IRI.
  3. The same license is recorded in the ontology's registry metadata.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: Add Annotation(dcterms:license <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/>) to the ontology header. The ontology template does this by default.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: The header of every file generated from the LOF ontology template declares CC BY 4.0.

docs.title: Criteria for review
docs.text:
The ontology header and the registry entry declare the same permitted license. Content derived from sources with incompatible licenses (for example, proprietary legal databases) is not included.

Automated check: ROBOT report check missing_ontology_license; registry schema validation of license.

docs.title: Feedback and discussion
docs.text: Propose changes to this principle by pull request against docs/principles/lof-p-001-open.md, or open a thread in Discussions.

docs.title: LOF-P-002: Common format
docs.text:
Draft for ratification

Part of the founding draft of the LOF principles.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The ontology is released in OWL 2, with a stable primary release file.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: A common format lets member ontologies import one another and lets the same tools (Protégé, ROBOT, reasoners, triple stores) operate on all of them.

docs.title: Recommendations and requirements
docs.text:
1. A release file lof-{id}.owl is published at the root of the ontology repository, serialized as RDF/XML or Turtle.
  2. A base file lof-{id}-base.owl, containing only the ontology's own axioms, is also published.
  3. Other serializations may be offered, but the OWL release is authoritative.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: Run make release VERSION=x.y.z in src/ontology/. The template Makefile produces both files with ROBOT.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: https://w3id.org/lof/odp-001.owl (full) and https://w3id.org/lof/odp-001/odp-001-base.owl (base).

docs.title: Criteria for review
docs.text:
Both release files exist, parse without error, and resolve through their persistent IRIs.

Automated check: CI parse and merge with ROBOT on every push.

docs.title: Feedback and discussion
docs.text: Propose changes to this principle by pull request against docs/principles/lof-p-002-format.md, or open a thread in Discussions.

docs.title: LOF-P-003: Common upper ontology
docs.text:
Draft for ratification

Part of the founding draft of the LOF principles.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The ontology is aligned to Basic Formal Ontology, and every class descends from a BFO class.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: A shared upper ontology is what makes independently developed ontologies interoperable. It guarantees that an obligation modeled in one ontology and a role modeled in another stand in well-defined relations to each other and to the physical and documentary entities they depend on.

docs.title: Recommendations and requirements
docs.text:
1. The ontology imports BFO 2020 (ISO/IEC 21838-2), or a module extracted from it.
  2. Every class in the ontology is a subclass, directly or through its ancestors, of a BFO class.
  3. BFO relations are used wherever they carry the intended meaning. Relations from the Relation Ontology (RO) or from other member ontologies are reused before new relations are minted.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: The template imports BFO 2020 core through src/ontology/imports/bfo_import.owl. Refresh it with make imports.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: A class legal role declared as a subclass of BFO role (BFO:0000023).

docs.title: Criteria for review
docs.text:
No class lacks a BFO ancestor. New relations are justified against existing BFO and RO relations.

Automated check: SPARQL check not-bfo-grounded-violation.

docs.title: Feedback and discussion
docs.text: Propose changes to this principle by pull request against docs/principles/lof-p-003-bfo.md, or open a thread in Discussions.

docs.title: LOF-P-004: Explicit grounding of legal entities
docs.text:
Draft for ratification

Part of the founding draft of the LOF principles.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Each top-level legal class states which BFO category it falls under, and why.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Legal entities such as obligations, rights, powers, legal persons, institutions, legal acts, and legal documents do not fit naive physical categories, and reasonable ontologists disagree about their placement. The Foundry does not settle every such dispute by fiat. It requires that each ontology make its choice explicit and defend it, so that alignment across ontologies is possible and disagreements are visible rather than hidden.

docs.title: Recommendations and requirements
docs.text:
1. Each top-level legal class (a class whose parent is a BFO class) has an rdfs:comment or linked documentation stating the rationale for its BFO placement.
  2. Where a Foundry design pattern (LOF-ODP) covers the modeling problem, the ontology uses it or documents why it departs from it.
  3. Placements that conflict with an accepted member ontology are raised with the Editorial Working Group before release.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: Record the rationale in the class annotation, and summarize the grounding decisions in a section of the ontology's README.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Legal obligation placed under generically dependent continuant on the ground that the same obligation can be concretized in many documents and survives the loss of any one of them; or under specifically dependent continuant, with a stated rationale. Either is acceptable if argued.

docs.title: Criteria for review
docs.text:
The reviewer can identify, for every top-level legal class, its BFO placement and the reason for it, and checks it against the LOF design patterns.

Automated check: None. Manual review.

docs.title: Feedback and discussion
docs.text: Propose changes to this principle by pull request against docs/principles/lof-p-004-grounding.md, or open a thread in Discussions.

docs.title: LOF-P-005: Persistent identifiers
docs.text:
Draft for ratification

Part of the founding draft of the LOF principles.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Every entity has a persistent IRI in the https://w3id.org/lof/ namespace, and IRIs are never reassigned or deleted.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Legal data annotated with an ontology term must mean the same thing years later. Identifiers that move, change meaning, or disappear silently corrupt every dataset that uses them.

docs.title: Recommendations and requirements
docs.text:
1. Term IRIs follow the pattern https://w3id.org/lof/{PREFIX}_{7 digits}, using the prefix reserved in the registry.
  2. Local identifiers are opaque and never encode the label.
  3. A term whose meaning changes gets a new IRI, and the old term is deprecated following the deprecation policy.
  4. Terms are never deleted from the ontology.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: Configure Protégé to generate IRIs from the editor's allocated ID range (see ID ranges).

docs.title: Examples

docs.title: Criteria for review
